c.tagline: Atlantic capital of Carnival, volcano views, and golden sand.

taxi.fareNote: Metered; Uber operates only in a limited way on the island, so licensed white street taxis and the Cabify app are the norm.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing spikes in Carnival crowds and around the bus interchange late at night.

hood_desc: The historic heart of the capital around Plaza de Espana and Plaza de la Candelaria, with pedestrian shopping streets, the Iglesia de la Concepcion, the TEA arts centre and the main Carnival route. Walkable and full of shops and tapas bars — the classic sightseeing base.

The modern seafront district south of the centre, defined by Calatrava's wave-shaped Auditorio de Tenerife, the Palmetum botanical garden and glass office towers around the Intercambiador transport hub. A well-connected, contemporary base right by the water.

A practical, well-located district just south of the centre around the Cuatro Torres and the La Salle shopping streets, with big-city amenities and quick access to both the old town and the waterfront. Convenient and good value for shoppers.

A whitewashed fishing village 7 km northeast of the city at the foot of the Anaga mountains, fronting the golden imported sand of Playa de Las Teresitas. Laid-back seafood terraces and beach days — quiet and scenic, a short bus ride from downtown.

Tenerife's UNESCO-listed former capital, a flat grid of pastel colonial mansions, churches and a big student population, linked to Santa Cruz by tram in about 40 minutes. Historic, atmospheric and lively in the evenings.

water.note: Officially potable but desalinated and mineral-heavy; most locals drink bottled for taste.

transit.hours: TITSA buses run from early morning to about 10-11pm on most routes, with limited night buses; the tram runs roughly 6am-midnight, and all night during Carnival and some weekends.
transit.note: The two tram lines link Santa Cruz with neighbouring San Cristobal de La Laguna; TITSA guaguas cover the whole island, including both airports and the road up to Mount Teide.
transit.pay: Get a rechargeable ten+ (tenmas) card from TITSA offices, kiosks and machines to tap on both the guaguas (TITSA buses) and the Tranvia tram at a big discount — a single tram ride is about EUR 1.35 with the card. Contactless bank cards are accepted on the tram; cash singles are paid to the bus driver.

landmarks: Auditorio de Tenerife
Santiago Calatrava's gravity-defying white wave crests over the harbour, an opera house as emblematic to Tenerife as Sydney's is to Australia.
Playa de Las Teresitas
Golden Saharan sand imported in the 1970s fills this palm-backed crescent beneath the Anaga mountains, the city's beloved swimming beach.
Plaza de España
The city's monumental waterfront square centres on a shallow artificial lake by Herzog & de Meuron, built over a former fortress.
Parque García Sanabria
A subtropical garden-park of flame trees, fountains and outdoor sculpture, crowned by its famous floral clock and shaded promenades.
Mercado de Nuestra Señora de África
A 1944 arcaded market of patios and clock tower where locals buy cheeses, mojo sauces and tropical fruit each morning.
Palmetum de Santa Cruz
A former landfill spectacularly reborn as the world's finest palm collection, with ocean panoramas from its landscaped hilltop.
Iglesia de la Concepción
The city's oldest church, a five-nave 16th-century treasure whose Moorish-style bell tower has long served as Santa Cruz's symbol.
Museo de la Naturaleza y Arqueología (MUNA)
Housed in a neoclassical former hospital, its star exhibits are the mummies and material culture of Tenerife's aboriginal Guanches.
TEA (Tenerife Espacio de las Artes)
A striking Herzog & de Meuron culture hub containing contemporary galleries, the Óscar Domínguez surrealist collection and a 24-hour library.
Parque Rural de Anaga
Ancient laurel cloud-forests, knife-edge ridges and hidden hamlets fill this UNESCO biosphere reserve rising directly behind the city.

train.note: The Canary Islands have no railways - a Tenerife line has been proposed for years but never built. Santa Cruz has two modern tram lines linking it with La Laguna, but for anything beyond the city you travel by bus, car or ferry.

bus.note: No international or mainland coach routes exist from an island. TITSA (https://www.titsa.com/en/) runs the green island-wide bus network from the Intercambiador in Santa Cruz to Puerto de la Cruz, Los Cristianos, Teide National Park and the airports; a Ten+ travel card cuts fares sharply.

ferry.note: Santa Cruz's harbour is right beside the city centre and is the main inter-island hub for the western Canaries. Fred. Olsen's fast ferries are quicker and Armas cheaper; the long mainland crossings to Cádiz and Huelva take a day and a half and carry cars. Note that many of the fast services to La Gomera and Los Cristianos leave from the south of the island rather than from Santa Cruz - check your ticket.

half.name: Teide National Park
half.blurb: Spain's highest peak rises from a volcanic caldera of lava fields and lunar rock formations, reachable by cable car near the summit.

half.name: Puerto de la Cruz
half.blurb: A resort town on the island's north coast with black-sand beaches, botanical gardens, and volcanic-rock swimming pools designed by César Manrique.

half.name: Garachico
half.blurb: A former port town rebuilt after a 1706 volcanic eruption buried its harbor, with natural lava-rock swimming pools along the shore.

full.name: Masca
full.blurb: A cliffside village at the head of a steep gorge in the Teno mountains, reached by a winding road with hairpin turns.
